<description>
There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.

This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable. Clean this up by setting `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer).

This is a slight behaviour change on Linux, but i think a desirable one. First of all because if a peer is sending us funky data we might as well hear about it and disconnect them, but also because i think one lesson to draw from the recent [socket related security vulnerability](https://bitcoincore.org/en/2026/10/28/disclose-tcp-oom/) is that we should reduce the amount of custom logic for less well-tested platforms.

Failing to set `SO_OOBINLINE` was conservatively made a warning and not a failure, because its absence does not prevent node operations, it's just annoying.
</description>

[2026-10-29] c:6509375262 comment by darosior (member):
The patch here is correct, but insufficient to address the issue entirely on macOS/BSD.

This comment from @pinheadmz got me wondering:

[quoted text omitted]
So i checked this as part of my socket tests hardening work, and it turns out that if you also set the urgent data pointer in the TCP segment header past the last byte you sent, `select()` on macOS / BSD keeps waking up while the socket is waiting to receive, until data past the mark has been read. Testing this is annoying (and can't reliably be done in our test suite) because the socket API won't let you set that pointer arbitrarily. So this requires writing IP packets directly in a raw socket, or some more involved hackery on Windows [^1].

So a peer receiving such a packet on:
 - Linux is unaffected (`poll()` without `POLLPRI`)
 - Windows will not raise the exception set (with `SO_OOBINLINE`)
 - macOS will raise the exception set (it does so as soon as it sees the pointer, even if the byte itself hasn't arrived yet, regardless of  `SO_OOBINLINE`)

Thankfully the exception set is only necessary on Windows, to detect a failed connection attempt. So we could `ifdef` it away, which would fix the macOS/BSD issue. But this is a bigger change, and i think the right solution is to just move to using `poll()` for all platforms.

Given the patch in this PR is simple, reviewed, and already fixes Windows, i think the complete fix for macOS should happen in a followup that either switches it to using `poll()` or gates the exception set to only be set for Windows.

[^1]: My bot was able to test this by crafting Ethernet frame and sending them to QEMU over UDP for it to inject them into the emulated NIC of the Windows VM.. Whatever.
